Reference: Acemoglu et al. (2012); Paper Link

Model Setting

Can idiosyncratic shocks to individual sectors generate sizable aggregate fluctuations? The standard answer, the diversification argument of Lucas (1977), is no: in an economy of nnn sectors hit by independent shocks, aggregate fluctuations have a magnitude proportional to 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​, which is negligible at high levels of disaggregation. Acemoglu, Carvalho, Ozdaglar and Tahbaz-Salehi (2012) show that this argument ignores input-output linkages, which propagate a shock from a sector to its customers, to the customers of its customers, and so on. In a static multisector model in the tradition of Long and Plosser (1983), with Cobb-Douglas preferences and technologies, the log of aggregate output is a weighted sum of the log sectoral shocks, and the weights form the influence vector, which depends only on the labour share and the input-output matrix. Aggregate volatility is therefore of the order of the Euclidean norm of the influence vector, and the question becomes how fast this norm decays as the economy is disaggregated, that is, along a sequence of economies with n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞.

The paper characterizes this rate of decay in terms of structural properties of the intersectoral network. Three theorems carry the argument. A lower bound in terms of the coefficient of variation of sectoral outdegrees shows that volatility decays more slowly when a few sectors supply a disproportionate share of all inputs (first-order interconnections); with a power-law degree distribution of shape parameter β∈(1,2)\beta\in(1,2)β∈(1,2), volatility is of order at least n−(β−1)/βn^{-(\beta-1)/\beta}n−(β−1)/β. A tighter bound adds a second-order interconnectivity coefficient, which is large when high-degree sectors share common suppliers and captures cascade effects; with a power-law second-order degree distribution of shape parameter ζ∈(1,2)\zeta\in(1,2)ζ∈(1,2), volatility is of order at least n−(ζ−1)/ζn^{-(\zeta-1)/\zeta}n−(ζ−1)/ζ. Conversely, in balanced structures, where no sector's degree grows with nnn, volatility decays at the rate 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ whenever the labour share is large enough, so that what matters is the asymmetry between sectors as suppliers and not the sparseness of the input-output matrix. In the US benchmark input-output tables for 1972 to 2002, both degree distributions have Pareto tails, with average estimates of 1.38 for the first-order and 1.18 for the second-order shape parameter. The latter implies that volatility decays no faster than n−0.15n^{-0.15}n−0.15, and a back-of-the-envelope calculation turns a sectoral standard deviation of 0.058 into an aggregate standard deviation of about 0.018, close to the roughly 2 percent standard deviation of US GDP.

where ℓi\ell_iℓi​ is labour hired by the sector, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)α∈(0,1) is the share of labour, xijx_{ij}xij​ is the amount of good jjj used in the production of good iii, and ziz_izi​ is the idiosyncratic productivity shock of sector iii. The input-output matrix WWW collects the wijw_{ij}wij​, and an economy is the tuple E=(I,W,{Fi}i∈I)\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{I},W,\{F_i\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}})E=(I,W,{Fi​}i∈I​) with I={1,2,…,n}\mathcal{I}=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}I={1,2,…,n} the set of sectors. By Assumption 1 every weighted indegree equals one, so the degrees sum to nnn and the average degree is one.

The influence of a sector is a common baseline α/n\alpha/nα/n plus 1−α1-\alpha1−α times the influence of its customers weighted by their input shares, which is why vvv is closely related to the Bonacich centrality vector of the intersectoral network: sectors with more direct or indirect downstream customers matter more for aggregate output. The term of order kkk in the series counts weighted supply chains of length kkk that start at a sector. Shocks propagate downstream only: a negative shock to a sector raises its price, which raises its demand for inputs, and lowers its output, which reduces that demand, and with Cobb-Douglas technologies the two effects on upstream sectors cancel.

The influence vector is also the sales vector. This matches the theorem of Hulten (1978), by which a productivity change d(αεi)d(\alpha\varepsilon_i)d(αεi​) changes the log of GDP by sales over GDP times that change; since h=α∑i=1npixih=\alpha\sum_{i=1}^np_ix_ih=α∑i=1n​pi​xi​, the result is dlog⁡(h)/dεi=vid\log(h)/d\varepsilon_i=v_idlog(h)/dεi​=vi​. The weights are sales shares and not sales divided by value added because the shocks are Harrod-neutral (ziz_izi​ is raised to the power α\alphaα). The link to sales connects the paper to the granular hypothesis of Gabaix (2011), with two differences: here the size distribution is derived from input-output linkages, and the network also determines sectoral comovement. Aggregate Volatility

Aggregate output, the influence vector, the entries of the matrix and the degrees of economy nnn are written yny_nyn​, vnv_nvn​, wijnw_{ij}^nwijn​ and dind_i^ndin​. Assumption 2 states that the log shocks εin\varepsilon_{in}εin​ have mean zero and variances σin2∈(σ‾2,σˉ2)\sigma_{in}^2\in(\underline{\sigma}^2,\bar{\sigma}^2)σin2​∈(σ​2,σˉ2), where 0<σ‾<σˉ0<\underline{\sigma}<\bar{\sigma}0<σ​<σˉ are independent of nnn; bounded variances isolate the role of the network from that of the decay of idiosyncratic volatility. For sequences of positive numbers, an=O(bn)a_n=O(b_n)an​=O(bn​) means lim sup⁡n→∞an/bn<∞\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_n/b_n<\inftylimsupn→∞​an​/bn​<∞, an=Ω(bn)a_n=\Omega(b_n)an​=Ω(bn​) means lim inf⁡n→∞an/bn>0\liminf_{n\to\infty}a_n/b_n>0liminfn→∞​an​/bn​>0, an=Θ(bn)a_n=\Theta(b_n)an​=Θ(bn​) means that both hold, and an=o(bn)a_n=o(b_n)an​=o(bn​) means lim⁡n→∞an/bn=0\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n/b_n=0limn→∞​an​/bn​=0. By independence, the standard deviation of aggregate output, called aggregate volatility, is:

(var yn)1/2=∑i=1nσin2vin2(4.11.5.12)(\text{var}\,y_n)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_{in}^2v_{in}^2} \tag{4.11.5.12}(varyn​)1/2=i=1∑n​σin2​vin2​​(4.11.5.12)

and therefore, under Assumption 2:

(var yn)1/2=Θ(∥vn∥2)(4.11.5.13)(\text{var}\,y_n)^{1/2}=\Theta\left(\|v_n\|_2\right) \tag{4.11.5.13}(varyn​)1/2=Θ(∥vn​∥2​)(4.11.5.13)

Aggregate volatility scales with the Euclidean norm of the influence vector. Since the elements of vnv_nvn​ are nonnegative and sum to one, ∥vn∥2≥1/n\|v_n\|_2\geq1/\sqrt{n}∥vn​∥2​≥1/n​, with equality when all sectors have the same influence; this is the diversification benchmark, obtained both in the economy without any linkages and in the complete network in which every sector relies equally on all others. The opposite extreme is the star network, in which sector 1 is the sole input supplier of all sectors. There vn′=αn1′+[(1−α),0,…,0]v_n'=\frac{\alpha}{n}\mathbf{1}'+[(1-\alpha),0,\ldots,0]vn′​=nα​1′+[(1−α),0,…,0], so ∥vn∥2=Θ(1)\|v_n\|_2=\Theta(1)∥vn​∥2​=Θ(1) and aggregate volatility does not vanish as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞: the law of large numbers fails. In general, the law of large numbers fails only if the influence of some sector, ∥vn∥∞\|v_n\|_{\infty}∥vn​∥∞​, stays bounded away from zero.

Asymptotic Distributions

which holds in two cases. In part (a) the shocks εin\varepsilon_{in}εin​ are normally distributed, and the result is immediate. In part (b) the distributions have uniformly dominated tails, meaning that there are a constant a>0a>0a>0 and a random variable εˉ\bar{\varepsilon}εˉ with bounded variance and distribution function Fˉ\bar{F}Fˉ such that Fin(x)<Fˉ(x)F_{in}(x)<\bar{F}(x)Fin​(x)<Fˉ(x) for all x<−ax<-ax<−a and Fin(x)>Fˉ(x)F_{in}(x)>\bar{F}(x)Fin​(x)>Fˉ(x) for all x>ax>ax>a, and in addition ∥vn∥∞/∥vn∥2→0\|v_n\|_{\infty}/\|v_n\|_2\to0∥vn​∥∞​/∥vn​∥2​→0. Part (c) is a converse: if the shocks are identically but not normally distributed and ∥vn∥∞/∥vn∥2\|v_n\|_{\infty}/\|v_n\|_2∥vn​∥∞​/∥vn​∥2​ does not converge to zero, then the asymptotic distribution of yn/∥vn∥2y_n/\|v_n\|_2yn​/∥vn​∥2​, when it exists, is nonnormal with finite variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. The network therefore governs both the rate of convergence and, unless all shocks are normal, the shape of the limiting distribution: when the most central sector remains non-negligible relative to the Euclidean norm, the distribution of aggregate output inherits the specific distribution of the sectoral shocks.

The proof of part (b) writes yn/(σ∥vn∥2)y_n/(\sigma\|v_n\|_2)yn​/(σ∥vn​∥2​) as the sum of the triangular array ξin=vinεin/(σ∥vn∥2)\xi_{in}=v_{in}\varepsilon_{in}/(\sigma\|v_n\|_2)ξin​=vin​εin​/(σ∥vn​∥2​), whose variances sum to one, and verifies Lindeberg's condition: the truncation threshold for εin\varepsilon_{in}εin​ is at least δσ∥vn∥2/∥vn∥∞\delta\sigma\|v_n\|_2/\|v_n\|_{\infty}δσ∥vn​∥2​/∥vn​∥∞​, which diverges, and the dominated tails make the truncated second moments vanish uniformly, so the Lindeberg-Feller theorem applies. Part (c) uses a nonclassical central limit theorem of Rotar (1975), whose necessary condition for normality fails when a single term keeps a non-vanishing share of the variance.

Intuitively, when the coefficient of variation is high, a small fraction of sectors is responsible for most input supplies, and their shocks reach all of their downstream customers. In the star network CVn=Θ(n)\text{CV}_n=\Theta(\sqrt{n})CVn​=Θ(n​), so volatility is bounded below by a constant; more generally, a dominant sector whose degree grows linearly with nnn prevents volatility from vanishing.

The first bound is a condition on the tail of the empirical degree distribution. A sequence of economies has a power law degree sequence if there exist a constant β>1\beta>1β>1, a slowly varying function L(⋅)L(\cdot)L(⋅) with lim⁡t→∞L(t)tδ=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}L(t)t^{\delta}=\inftylimt→∞​L(t)tδ=∞ and lim⁡t→∞L(t)t−δ=0\lim_{t\to\infty}L(t)t^{-\delta}=0limt→∞​L(t)t−δ=0 for all δ>0\delta>0δ>0, and positive numbers cn=Θ(1)c_n=\Theta(1)cn​=Θ(1) such that, for all nnn and all k<dmax⁡n=Θ(n1/β)k<d_{\max}^n=\Theta(n^{1/\beta})k<dmaxn​=Θ(n1/β):

Pn(k)=cnk−βL(k)(4.11.5.19)P_n(k)=c_nk^{-\beta}L(k) \tag{4.11.5.19}Pn​(k)=cn​k−βL(k)(4.11.5.19)

where Pn(k)≡1n∣{i∈In:din>k}∣P_n(k)\equiv\frac{1}{n}|\{i\in\mathcal{I}_n:d_i^n>k\}|Pn​(k)≡n1​∣{i∈In​:din​>k}∣ is the empirical counter-cumulative distribution function and dmax⁡nd_{\max}^ndmaxn​ is the maximum degree. A lower shape parameter β\betaβ means a heavier tail. Corollary 1: if the shape parameter is β∈(1,2)\beta\in(1,2)β∈(1,2), then for arbitrary δ>0\delta>0δ>0:

(var yn)1/2=Ω(n−(β−1)/β−δ)(4.11.5.20)(\text{var}\,y_n)^{1/2}=\Omega\left(n^{-(\beta-1)/\beta-\delta}\right) \tag{4.11.5.20}(varyn​)1/2=Ω(n−(β−1)/β−δ)(4.11.5.20)

The proof writes the sum of squared degrees as an integral of the counter-cumulative distribution up to dmax⁡nd_{\max}^ndmaxn​, which for β<2\beta<2β<2 is governed by the largest degrees. As β\betaβ approaches 1 volatility hardly decays at all, and as β\betaβ approaches 2 the bound approaches the diversification rate n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2. These results are lower bounds only: even with a thin-tailed degree distribution, higher-order properties of the network can keep volatility from decaying at the rate 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​.

Second-Order Interconnections and Cascades

Two economies with identical degree sequences can have very different volatility. Example 2 compares sequences {En}n∈N\{\mathcal{E}_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}{En​}n∈N​ and {E^n}n∈N\{\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}{En​}n∈N​ in which every edge has weight one. It measures the extent to which sectors with high degrees are connected to one another through common suppliers: by the rearrangement inequality it is larger when high-degree sectors share suppliers with other high-degree sectors than when they share them with low-degree ones. Balanced Structures

A partial converse holds when the variation in degrees is limited. A sequence of economies is balanced if max⁡i∈Indin=Θ(1)\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}_n}d_i^n=\Theta(1)maxi∈In​​din​=Θ(1), so that no sector's degree increases without bound; this is the polar opposite of a network with a dominant sector. Theorem 4: for a sequence of balanced economies there exists αˉ∈(0,1)\bar{\alpha}\in(0,1)αˉ∈(0,1) such that, for α≥αˉ\alpha\geq\bar{\alpha}α≥αˉ, (var yn)1/2=Θ(1/n)(\text{var}\,y_n)^{1/2}=\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})(varyn​)1/2=Θ(1/n​). The lower bound ∥vn∥2=Ω(1/n)\|v_n\|_2=\Omega(1/\sqrt{n})∥vn​∥2​=Ω(1/n​) holds for any sequence. For the upper bound, the induced 1-norm of the matrix is its largest column sum, ∥Wn∥1=max⁡i∈Indin≤C\|W_n\|_1=\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}_n}d_i^n\leq C∥Wn​∥1​=maxi∈In​​din​≤C for a constant CCC independent of nnn, and the recursive form of the influence vector gives ∥vn∥∞≤αn+(1−α)C∥vn∥∞\|v_n\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\alpha}{n}+(1-\alpha)C\|v_n\|_{\infty}∥vn​∥∞​≤nα​+(1−α)C∥vn​∥∞​. Hence, for α>(C−1)/C\alpha>(C-1)/Cα>(C−1)/C:

∥vn∥∞≤αn[1−(1−α)C]−1(4.11.5.30)\|v_n\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\alpha}{n}\left[1-(1-\alpha)C\right]^{-1} \tag{4.11.5.30}∥vn​∥∞​≤nα​[1−(1−α)C]−1(4.11.5.30)

so ∥vn∥∞=O(1/n)\|v_n\|_{\infty}=O(1/n)∥vn​∥∞​=O(1/n), and Holder's inequality ∥vn∥2≤∥vn∥1∥vn∥∞\|v_n\|_2\leq\sqrt{\|v_n\|_1\|v_n\|_{\infty}}∥vn​∥2​≤∥vn​∥1​∥vn​∥∞​​ with ∥vn∥1=1\|v_n\|_1=1∥vn​∥1​=1 gives ∥vn∥2=O(1/n)\|v_n\|_2=O(1/\sqrt{n})∥vn​∥2​=O(1/n​). When the network is balanced and intermediate inputs are not too important, no other structural property can add to volatility, and aggregate fluctuations do not have network origins. Structures often regarded as fragile, such as the ring and the binary tree, behave asymptotically like the empty and the complete network. Sparseness of the input-output matrix is therefore irrelevant, contrary to the conjecture of Horvath (1998); only asymmetry in the roles of sectors, first-order or higher-order, lets sectoral shocks drive aggregate fluctuations. The theorem generalizes Dupor (1999) and is both an aggregation result (a balanced multisector economy is observationally equivalent to a one-sector economy) and an irrelevance result (all balanced input-output matrices generate roughly the same volatility); neither interpretation survives when the network is not balanced.

Application to the US Input-Output Tables

The data are the detailed benchmark input-output accounts of the Bureau of Economic Analysis, compiled every five years from 1972 to 2002. The commodity-by-commodity direct requirements tables give the value of spending on one commodity per dollar of production of another at current producer prices; they are the finest disaggregation available, with most sectors roughly at the four-digit SIC level (SIC-based until 1992, NAICS from 1997) and between 417 and 529 sectors per year.

  • Indegrees: the intermediate input share averages 0.55 across years and sectors, between 0.52 in 1987 and 0.58 in 2002, and on average 71 percent of sectors lie within one standard deviation of the mean. The model's assumption of a common intermediate share 1−α1-\alpha1−α is thus a reasonable approximation. To obtain the counterpart of WWW, each entry is divided by the total input requirement of the purchasing sector, so that mean first-order and second-order degrees equal one; the results are unchanged without this step.

  • Outdegrees: the empirical distributions of did_idi​ and qiq_iqi​ are strongly right-skewed, in contrast to the indegrees. Some commodities are general purpose inputs, and others are major suppliers of the sectors that produce them. The five highest first-order degrees belong to management of companies and enterprises, wholesale trade, real estate, electric power generation, transmission and distribution, and iron and steel mills; the five highest second-order degrees belong to the first three of these, advertising, and monetary authorities and depository credit intermediation.

  • Shape parameters: on a log-log scale the counter-cumulative distributions are approximately linear in the tail, taken as the top 20 percent of sectors. The modified log rank-log size regression of Gabaix and Ibragimov (2011), which corrects the small-sample bias of ordinary least squares, gives for 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997 and 2002 estimates of β\betaβ equal to 1.38, 1.38, 1.35, 1.37, 1.32, 1.43 and 1.46 (standard errors 0.18 to 0.23), and estimates of ζ\zetaζ equal to 1.14, 1.15, 1.10, 1.14, 1.15, 1.27 and 1.30 (standard errors 0.15 to 0.20). The averages are β^=1.38\hat{\beta}=1.38β^​=1.38 and ζ^=1.18\hat{\zeta}=1.18ζ^​=1.18, and the second-order estimate is below the first-order one in every year. Slopes from a Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression average 1.28 and 1.17, Hill-type maximum likelihood estimates following Clauset, Shalizi and Newman (2009) average 1.39 and 1.14, and the tables without normalization give 1.42 and 1.23.

  • Norm of the influence vector: at the detailed level ∥vnd∥2\|v_{n_d}\|_2∥vnd​​∥2​ lies between 0.088 and 0.098 across years (0.098 in 1972 with nd=483n_d=483nd​=483, 0.094 in 2002 with nd=417n_d=417nd​=417), roughly twice 1/nd1/\sqrt{n_d}1/nd​​, so linkages at least double the impact of sectoral shocks. At the summary level (80 to 128 sectors) ∥vns∥2\|v_{n_s}\|_2∥vns​​∥2​ lies between 0.115 and 0.149. The ratio ∥vnd∥2/∥vns∥2\|v_{n_d}\|_2/\|v_{n_s}\|_2∥vnd​​∥2​/∥vns​​∥2​ is 0.705, 0.664, 0.591, 0.662, 0.679, 0.783 and 0.790 in the seven years, always above the diversification benchmark (1/nd)/(1/ns)(1/\sqrt{n_d})/(1/\sqrt{n_s})(1/nd​​)/(1/ns​​) of 0.417, 0.400, 0.399, 0.418, 0.432, 0.518 and 0.554. In 1972, moving from 84 to 483 sectors should lower the role of sectoral shocks by 58 percent under the diversification argument, whereas the observed decline is about 29 percent.

  • Implied decay rates: by Corollary 2, ζ^=1.18\hat{\zeta}=1.18ζ^​=1.18 implies volatility of order at least n−(ζ−1)/ζ=n−0.15n^{-(\zeta-1)/\zeta}=n^{-0.15}n−(ζ−1)/ζ=n−0.15, a tighter bound than the n−(β−1)/β=n−0.28n^{-(\beta-1)/\beta}=n^{-0.28}n−(β−1)/β=n−0.28 implied by β^=1.38\hat{\beta}=1.38β^​=1.38, and far slower than n−0.5n^{-0.5}n−0.5. The rate is consistent with the declines in the norm between the summary and the detailed level.

  • Back-of-the-envelope volatility: the average standard deviation of total factor productivity across 459 four-digit SIC manufacturing industries in the NBER productivity database for 1958 to 2005, after removing a linear trend, is 0.058 (0.054 with weights equal to log value added). Manufacturing is about 20 percent of GDP, so the economy is treated as 5×459=22955\times459=22955×459=2295 sectors at this level of disaggregation. Under the rate of a balanced structure aggregate volatility would be about 0.058/2295≈0.0010.058/\sqrt{2295}\approx0.0010.058/2295​≈0.001; under the rate n−0.15n^{-0.15}n−0.15 it is 0.058/22950.15≈0.0180.058/2295^{0.15}\approx0.0180.058/22950.15≈0.018, in the range of the approximately 2 percent standard deviation of US GDP.

The extrapolation assumes that the power law tail of the second-order degrees persists at finer levels of disaggregation, which the scale-free shape of the distribution suggests and the data cannot confirm. The paper presents these calculations as suggestive, and not as a substitute for a systematic quantitative analysis. It also treats the network as an exogenous technological constraint; endogenous choice of suppliers, large deviations of output from its mean, and contagion in financial networks are left for further research.

This is the utility function of the representative household: a Cobb-Douglas aggregate of the nnn goods in which every good has the same exponent 1/n1/n1/n. Here cic_ici​ is the quantity of good iii consumed and A>0A>0A>0 is a constant that only rescales utility; it is chosen in equation (7) so that log real GDP has no constant term.

The functional form buys two things. First, the household spends the same fraction 1/n1/n1/n of its income on each good whatever the prices. With income equal to the wage hhh (one unit of labour, zero profits), maximizing uuu subject to ∑i=1npici=h\sum_{i=1}^np_ic_i=h∑i=1n​pi​ci​=h gives

ci=hnpi,u=A∏i=1n(hnpi)1/n=hnA(p1p2⋯pn)1/nc_i=\frac{h}{np_i},\qquad u=A\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{h}{np_i}\right)^{1/n}=\frac{h}{\frac{n}{A}\left(p_1p_2\cdots p_n\right)^{1/n}}ci​=npi​h​,u=Ai=1∏n​(npi​h​)1/n=An​(p1​p2​⋯pn​)1/nh​

so indirect utility is the wage divided by an ideal price index, which is what equations (7) and (8) use. Second, because the weights are equal, no sector is more important than another as a supplier of final goods: any asymmetry in the influence vector of equation (9) comes from the input-output matrix alone. The unit elasticity of substitution rules out any reallocation of final expenditure in response to shocks, which is why the final-demand term in the sales recursion behind equation (11) is the constant h/nh/nh/n.

This is the production technology of sector iii. Output xix_ixi​ is Cobb-Douglas in labour ℓi\ell_iℓi​, with exponent α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)α∈(0,1), and in a Cobb-Douglas bundle of intermediate inputs xijx_{ij}xij​, with exponents (1−α)wij(1-\alpha)w_{ij}(1−α)wij​. The weight wij≥0w_{ij}\geq0wij​≥0 is the share of good jjj in the intermediate input bill of sector iii, and Assumption 1, ∑j=1nwij=1\sum_{j=1}^nw_{ij}=1∑j=1n​wij​=1, makes the exponents sum to one:

α+(1−α)∑j=1nwij=1\alpha+(1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^nw_{ij}=1α+(1−α)j=1∑n​wij​=1

so the technology has constant returns to scale and competitive firms earn zero profits. Under cost minimization the cost shares are constant: labour receives the fraction α\alphaα of revenue and input jjj the fraction (1−α)wij(1-\alpha)w_{ij}(1−α)wij​, which is why wijw_{ij}wij​ can be read off an input-output table.

The shock ziz_izi​ enters as ziαz_i^{\alpha}ziα​, that is, it is labour-augmenting (Harrod-neutral); in logs sectoral total factor productivity is αεi\alpha\varepsilon_iαεi​ with εi=log⁡(zi)\varepsilon_i=\log(z_i)εi​=log(zi​). The Cobb-Douglas form implies that prices are log-linear in the shocks, equation (5), that the influence vector depends only on α\alphaα and WWW, equation (9), and that shocks do not propagate upstream. A special case: with α=1\alpha=1α=1 there are no linkages, xi=ziℓix_i=z_i\ell_ixi​=zi​ℓi​, and every sector has influence 1/n1/n1/n.

The degree did_idi​ is the sum of column iii of the input-output matrix WWW. The entry wjiw_{ji}wji​ is the share of good iii in the intermediate input bill of sector jjj, so did_idi​ adds up the input shares that sector iii holds across all of its customers jjj; it measures the importance of sector iii as a direct supplier. It is an outdegree because in the intersectoral network an edge of weight wjiw_{ji}wji​ runs from supplier iii to customer jjj.

The row sums of WWW are all equal to one by Assumption 1, whereas the column sums are unrestricted. Summing over all sectors,

∑i=1ndi=∑i=1n∑j=1nwji=∑j=1n(∑i=1nwji)=n\sum_{i=1}^nd_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nw_{ji}=\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{i=1}^nw_{ji}\right)=ni=1∑n​di​=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​wji​=j=1∑n​(i=1∑n​wji​)=n

Two examples: in the complete network with wij=1/nw_{ij}=1/nwij​=1/n, and in a ring, every degree equals one; in the star network, where sector 1 is the only supplier, d1=nd_1=nd1​=n and all other degrees are zero.

The degree is the first-order term of the influence vector: by equation (10), vi≥αn+α(1−α)ndiv_i\geq\frac{\alpha}{n}+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{n}d_ivi​≥nα​+nα(1−α)​di​. These are the market clearing conditions that close the competitive equilibrium. The first line says that the output xix_ixi​ of good iii is either consumed by the household, cic_ici​, or used as an intermediate input by some sector jjj; note the order of the subscripts, xjix_{ji}xji​ is the amount of good iii used by sector jjj, so the sum runs over the customers of sector iii. This equation defines a power law (Pareto) tail for the degree sequence. The second-order interconnectivity coefficient sums, over every sector iii and every ordered pair of distinct customers jjj and kkk of iii (both different from iii), the product of the two input shares wjinw_{ji}^nwjin​ and wkinw_{ki}^nwkin​ and of the degrees djnd_j^ndjn​ and dknd_k^ndkn​ of the two customers. A term is large when sector iii is an important supplier of two sectors that are themselves important suppliers. The coefficient is therefore high when high-degree sectors share common suppliers, so that a shock to the common supplier hits several hubs at once and then spreads to their many customers: a two-step cascade.
